sections.heading: Separate the release from the marketing campaign
sections.content: Let developers choose a release date that works for them; if it shifts, marketing need not shift its campaign with it. The product’s initial release is the soft launch. Once it is live, hold a launch meeting and plan the hard launch using the actual product rather than design images that may change or an uncertain release date.

sections.heading: Give marketing real material, and let development move on
sections.content: A working version gives marketing something it can share with customers, record videos of, and collect early beta-user testimonials about. Marketing can then spend the time it chooses—Bastow gives examples from two days to six months—planning the hard launch. During that period, development continues on its next project; when marketing is ready, it can coordinate around what has been built next.

sections.heading: Caveat for fixed-date launches
sections.content: For a launch tied to a deadline, such as the Christmas rush or the school year, Bastow recommends planning ahead and adding buffer so there is time for a soft launch, iteration, and fixes before the full launch. She cautions against applying this level of detailed planning to every launch, which can slow teams down.

answer.summary: Have development release a working version when it’s ready as a soft launch, then let marketing plan and run the hard launch once it can work from the real product. Meanwhile, development can move on to its next project, avoiding pressure to synchronize two different timelines.

sections.heading: Separate the releases and workstreams
sections.content: Let developers soft-launch the product on a date that works for development; the date may shift without forcing marketing to reset a major campaign. Once the working version is live, marketing can kick off its launch planning and choose how much time it needs for the hard launch. During that marketing period, development can continue building the next thing. This avoids the stress of trying to line up marketing and development projects with different schedules.

sections.heading: Give marketing something real to use
sections.content: After the soft launch, marketing can see the functional product rather than relying on designs that may change or an uncertain release date. It can share the working version with some customers and gather videos and testimonials from early beta users to support the hard launch.
